analysis.one_liner: Gives federal grants to states and cities that guarantee free lawyers to low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: A bill to help pay for lawyers for low-income tenants facing eviction was introduced in the Senate but never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal fund—$100 million a year for five years—that pays grants to states, cities, and tribal governments that pass laws giving free, full legal representation to tenants facing eviction if they earn up to twice the federal poverty level. It also favors applicants that add other tenant protections, like requiring 30 days' notice before eviction and limiting no-fault evictions. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income renters facing eviction—roughly tenants earning up to twice the federal poverty line—would get a lawyer at no cost in eviction and housing-subsidy cases, in any state or city that takes the federal money and passes a right-to-counsel law. Studies of existing right-to-counsel programs consistently find represented tenants far more likely to stay in their homes. Public legal aid programs and eviction-defense attorneys would also gain funded work.

how_it_helps.text: It establishes an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund, authorizing $100 million a year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029.

Grants go to states, local governments, and tribal governments that pass laws guaranteeing free, full legal representation to tenants earning up to 200% of the federal poverty line in eviction cases and subsidy-termination cases.

The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development must give priority to applicants that also protect tenants in other ways—limiting no-fault evictions, requiring at least 30 days' written notice, running eviction diversion programs, or providing emergency rental assistance—and to programs that recruit and train attorneys.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the $100 million annual appropriation; and landlords, who would face represented tenants and, in prioritized jurisdictions, new limits on no-fault evictions and lease non-renewals, plus a required 30-day notice period.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $100 million a year in new federal spending for five years, a cost supporters would need to justify against other housing priorities.
The grant bonus points reward limits on why landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease, which landlord groups generally oppose on the grounds that they make renting riskier and can raise costs.
Because grants flow only to governments that already pass right-to-counsel laws, low-income tenants in states and cities that decline to act would get no help from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: legal representation measurably reduces eviction judgments, and the bill targets the lowest-income renters at the moment they most need help. The main costs are fiscal—$100 million a year in new federal spending—and indirect: incentive grants could push cities to adopt landlord-notice restrictions, which landlords argue increase screening and rent costs. A design gap is that the money only follows states and cities that already pass right-to-counsel laws, so the most reluctant jurisdictions—the ones with the most unrepresented tenants—get nothing. On balance the bill's costs are modest and its aims concrete, but it never advanced far enough to be judged in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 9, 2024 and read twice in the Senate.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which is where the action history ends.
No further actions—no hearings, markup, committee report, or floor vote—are recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords facing possible new tenant-protection laws are better off; low-income tenants gained nothing because the program was never funded.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five colleagues to cosponsor it.

for.name: Sens. Van Hollen, Wyden, Warren, and Sanders

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats or left-leaning independents; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would fund legal defense for tenants challenging evictions, and its priority criteria favor governments that restrict no-fault evictions and require 30-day notice. Landlords in covered areas would face slower, costlier evictions, though tenants who keep housing also pay rent to landlords.
Grant funds can pay for training and recruiting attorneys to represent tenants, expanding paid work for the eviction-defense bar and legal aid organizations.
